extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the correctness and legitimacy of inferences, generalizations, and the role of the syllogism in scientific and everyday reasoning. Emphasizes when induction, general propositions, and syllogistic forms are appropriate and what errors to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference must be grounded in particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: "All inference is from particulars to particulars: General propositions are merely registers of such inferences already made, and short formulæ for making more."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real logical antecedent of any syllogistic conclusion are the particular facts from which the general proposition was collected by induction. Examples: concluding 'The Duke of Wellington is mortal' ultimately rests on observed individual deaths (John, Thomas, etc.). Practical and animal reasoning (burned child, burned dog, skilled workmen, warrior arranging troops) illustrate that inferences arise from remembered particulars, not from abstract generalities alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petitio principii (begging the question)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It must be granted that in every syllogism, considered as an argument to prove the conclusion, there is a _petitio principii_."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a general premise (e.g., 'All men are mortal') may presuppose the truth of the particular it is used to prove; ensure premises do not covertly assume the conclusion. The critic's objection is that a syllogism can 'prove no more than is involved in the premises.' Treat claims that appear circular with suspicion and examine the prior evidence for the general premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the act of inference from the act of registering/generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The text stresses the difference between the inferring part and the registering part, and warns against ascribing the origin of knowledge to one's notes or general statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked how a belief was reached, do not confuse having a memorandum or general formula with the original inductive process that produced the belief. Notes and definitions are memory aids; they are not the source of the inductive warrant (Koran/quill example). Evaluations should trace back to the observations and inferences, not only to recorded generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizations must be supported by sufficient instances
rubrics_metrics.description: "Generalization is not a process of mere naming, it is also a process of inference. From instances which we have observed, we feel warranted in concluding, that what we found true in those instances, holds in all similar ones..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the observed instances are numerous and representative enough to justify extending the inference to an indefinite class. Formulating the general theorem explicates the full extent of what the evidence must prove and helps test sufficiency of evidence before applying it to new cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generalization as a diagnostic to reveal insufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulating the whole class of possible inferences in a general proposition 'operates as a security for their being just' because a false generalization will often entail a contradiction with known facts (a reductio ad impossibile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering a proposed inference, restate it as a general proposition covering all analogous cases; then search for counterexamples within that class. The Commodus/Nero example shows how thinking in general terms can quickly reveal that premises are inadequate. This is an anti-bias technique: broad formulation makes hidden inadequacies visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the syllogism as an interpretive and consistency-checking tool
rubrics_metrics.description: "The rules of the syllogism are a set of precautions to insure our doing so" (reading the record correctly); the syllogism's function is 'to maintain consistency between the conclusions we draw in every particular case, and the previous general directions for drawing them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllogistic form not as the source of new empirical knowledge but as rules for interpreting and applying prior generalizations consistently. Evaluate reasoning by checking that particular conclusions conform to the intended scope of the general premises; the syllogism helps avoid drawing inferences outside the intended class.

rubrics_metrics.name: When premises come from authority, apply hermeneutics (interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the premises are given by testimony or command, the operation is 'a process of interpretation' — ascertain whether the authority intended to include the present case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authority-based generalities (testimony, law), evaluate whether the authoritative source's words, signs, or stated intent actually encompass the case at hand. This is crucial in legal or testimonial reasoning: the inquiry is whether the case 'possesses the marks' that the authority signified as falling under the general assertion or command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer making explicit general propositions to strengthen scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating a general principle 'in its broadest form of generality' forces us to consider the whole extent of what our evidence must prove and 'is felt as of greater importance' so the mind 'weigh[s] more carefully the sufficiency of the experience appealed to.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when one can reason directly from particulars to particulars, converting the inference into an explicit general proposition is often advantageous: it increases attention to evidentiary sufficiency and reduces the chance of wishful or negligent reasoning. Use explicit generalization as a methodological step to audit inference quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct particular-to-particular inference is valid but limited in communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: We often reason directly from particulars to particulars without forming general propositions (child learns to avoid fire, skilled workman cannot articulate rules), and such reasoning can be effective though non-verbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the legitimacy of tacit, experience-based judgment (practical skill, animals, seasoned practitioners). However, lack of explicit generalization makes such reasoning hard to justify or teach — prefer to translate tacit knowledge into stated principles when explanation or transfer is required (Lord Mansfield example).

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions are shorthand statements of assumptions, not metaphysical sources of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions, axioms, and laws are 'merely abridged statements' of particular assumptions; demonstrations often rest on particular assumed facts specific to the instance (diagram ABC) rather than on the general form alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proofs or demonstrations, remember that general axioms/definitions compress particular assumptions. A demonstration can often be understood as proving a particular case; the general theorem is a codification of many such demonstrations. Therefore, check the underlying particular assumptions that the general statement is meant to summarize.
